paragraphs.text: Disease caused by biallelic PNPLA8 variants has been described with a range of presentations. Abdel-Hamid et al. (2024) grouped them into 3 forms: a congenital form with congenital microcephaly, early-onset epileptic encephalopathy, and early death; childhood neurodegeneration with progressive microcephaly; and adult-onset cerebellar ataxia with peripheral neuropathy. Shukla et al. (2018) considered the disorder a progressive neurodegenerative mitochondrial disease. Nakamura et al. (2024) concluded that PNPLA8-related neurologic disease forms a continuum, ranging from developmental and/or degenerative epileptic-dyskinetic encephalopathy with congenital microcephaly to childhood-onset neurodegeneration.

He had a high-output circulatory state and cardiomyopathy that had caused cardiac insufficiency 22 years before the skeletal myopathy presented. Electron microscopy of muscle showed various mitochondrial abnormalities and an accumulation of neutral lipids, which was confirmed by histochemistry and thin-layer chromatography.

paragraphs.text: Saunders et al. (2015) reported a girl (CMH193) with progressive muscle weakness. Toe-walking was noted in her first year. At age 2 years she had a positive Gowers sign, and by age 3 years she could no longer walk. Other features included hypotonia, complex partial seizures, poor weight gain, a lean body habitus, dystonia, dysarthria, dysmetria, spasticity, and tight heel cords. Laboratory studies showed lactic acidosis with an elevated anion gap, elevated blood pyruvate, and CSF 5-methyltetrahydrofolate deficiency. Creatine phosphokinase was normal. Brain MRI showed increased signal in the medial globus pallidus. Muscle biopsy showed variable fiber size with atrophic fibers but no ragged red fibers. Electron microscopy showed abnormal mitochondrial cristae, osmiophilic inclusions, and subsarcolemmal aggregates of abnormal mitochondria. Respiratory chain function was normal. She was last reported at age 7 years.

paragraphs.text: Shukla et al. (2018) reported 2 unrelated girls with variable but similar features: microcephaly, severe global developmental delay, spasticity, lactic acidosis, and progressive cerebellar atrophy. Patient 1, the second child of a consanguineous Indian couple, was evaluated on the sixth postnatal day for congenital microcephaly and seizures. She had low birth weight, multifocal clonic seizures in the neonatal period, spasticity of all 4 limbs, and overriding cranial sutures. Brain MRI showed microcephaly with a simplified gyral pattern, hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, a prominent cisterna magna with a hypoplastic cerebellum, and brainstem atrophy. MR spectroscopy showed an elevated lipid-lactate peak. Patient 2, of Indian/Fijian ancestry and born to nonconsanguineous parents, developed normally until 13 months of age and then regressed. Her features included epilepsia partialis continua and focal seizures, severe global developmental delay, absent speech, gastrostomy tube feeding, central hypotonia, acquired microcephaly, choreiform movements, dystonia, proximal muscle weakness, absent muscle stretch reflexes, spasticity, and joint contractures. Brain MRI showed delayed myelination, progressive cerebellar atrophy, brainstem and cerebral atrophy, and a thin corpus callosum, and MR spectroscopy showed an elevated lipid-lactate peak. EEG showed multifocal epileptiform discharges with background slowing, and visual evoked potentials were abnormal. Echocardiography detected hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with subaortic stenosis. Blood lactate was elevated on several occasions, and GDF15 was elevated. She also had obstructive sleep apnea and restrictive lung disease. Muscle electron microscopy showed enlarged, irregular mitochondria, but respiratory chain complex I-IV activities were normal. She was last reported at age 15 years.

paragraphs.text: Burnyte et al. (2023) reported 2 Lithuanian adult sibs with adolescent-onset cerebellar ataxia and sensorimotor polyneuropathy. The disease advanced markedly in their teens and progressed only slightly in adulthood. Cognition was preserved, and there was no visual, auditory, cardiac, or liver dysfunction. The brother, aged 49 years at last report, first developed lower limb weakness and distal lower limb muscle atrophy at age 14 years and became nonambulant at age 44. Examination at 45 years showed mild dysarthria and horizontal nystagmus. Other findings were axial ataxia, tetraparesis, decreased muscle tone, absent lower limb tendon reflexes, foot deformities, bilateral Babinski signs, dysmetria, length-dependent hypoesthesia in the lower limbs, and sensorimotor axonal polyneuropathy. Brain imaging showed mild cerebellar atrophy, and laboratory studies were normal. His sister, aged 21 years at last report, developed difficulty walking and weakness of both lower limbs at age 14 years. She had distal upper and lower limb muscle atrophy, absent lower limb tendon reflexes, bilateral Babinski signs, severe axial ataxia, and appendicular dysmetria that was more pronounced in the lower limbs. She was unable to maintain an upright posture and had an axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy. Cranial nerve examination and cognitive evaluation were normal, and EMG showed no myopathic changes.

paragraphs.text: Nakamura et al. (2024) reported 14 new patients with biallelic PNPLA8 variants. In the 12 families with neurologic disease, they found central hypotonia (13 of 13), dystonia (8 of 12), seizures (10 of 14), and cerebellar atrophy (12 of 12). The 8 severely affected patients (patients 1 to 8) were from Japan (2), Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Afghanistan, Pakistan, Turkey, and Lebanon, and all but the 2 Japanese patients were born to consanguineous parents. Families 7 and 8 had been reported previously. These patients had congenital microcephaly (5 of 7), no developmental milestones, early-onset seizures (beginning between day 1 and 7 months of age), a simplified gyral pattern, pontocerebellar hypoplasia, and progressive cerebral atrophy. Patient 1 died at 4 years, patient 2 at 10 months, and patient 8 at 8 months of age. The patients from families 9 and 10 had intermediate severity, with cerebellar atrophy that was very mild in patient 10. Four patients had a relatively mild phenotype: 3 Iranian sibs born to consanguineous parents (family 11) and an Egyptian woman born to consanguineous parents (family 12). All 4 attained walking (4 of 4) and then had regression of milestones (4 of 4). They also had ataxia (3 of 4), mild or no intellectual disability (3 of 4), and isolated or absent seizures (4 of 4), together with hypotonia, dystonia, a neuromuscular disorder, and cerebellar atrophy. One of the sibs in family 11 had seizures from age 31 years. Nakamura et al. (2024) also reviewed 25 affected individuals from 20 families with biallelic PNPLA8 variants.

paragraphs.text: Nakamura et al. (2024) identified biallelic PNPLA8 variants in 12 families with neurologic disease. All 14 variants they identified had frequencies below 0.001% in population databases. In patient-derived lymphoblastoid cell lines, the c.1625+3_1625+6del variant from patient 1 caused skipping of exons 6 to 8. On immunoblotting, skin fibroblasts from patient 1 showed a marked reduction in the 77-kDa PNPLA8 protein, indicating a null effect. The splicing effects of c.2075-2A-G (patient 2) and c.1684-2A-G (patient 5) could not be tested. The frameshift variant p.Glu296LysfsTer6 in severely affected patient 6 also had a null effect. In contrast, patient 12, who had a mild phenotype and the p.Leu759AlafsTer4 variant, showed weak expression of the 77-kDa protein, suggesting residual protein function. The missense variant from a previously reported severely affected patient (homozygous p.Val520Asp) gave normal protein levels.
